assessment.rationale: Span 25 states HEAD requests metadata headers only; span 28 warns that if a HEAD response has a body it must be ignored. Together they describe that a HEAD response has no response content body, per the specification's design.
assessment.provenance_note: MDN page references the HTTP Semantics specification for HEAD method definition.
limitations: No explicit citation of the June 2022 published worldwide HTTP standard

excerpts.text: The **`HEAD`** HTTP method requests the metadata of a resource in the form of [headers](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers) that the server would have sent if the [`GET`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET) method was used instead.

**Warning:** If a response to a `HEAD` request has a body, the response body must be ignored. Any [representation headers](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Representation_header) that describe the erroneous body are assumed to describe the response body that a `GET` request would have received.

assessment.rationale: Span 69 lists the HTTP Semantics #HEAD specification at httpwg.org, which is the worldwide HTTP standard. No date is given in the span, but the specification cited is the current HTTP standard.
assessment.provenance_note: Span 69 links to the HTTP Semantics specification.
limitations: No publication date extracted from span

assessment.rationale: Span 131 states the HEAD method is identical to GET except the server MUST NOT return a message-body in the response. Span 132 confirms the server MUST NOT return a message-body. The text states no response body is included, not that there is 'no response content' overall, as headers are still sent.

limitations: Does not address header content explicitly

excerpts.text: # [HEAD being handled as GET by default is not cheap...](/t/head-being-handled-as-get-by-default-is-not-cheap/22271)
The **HTTP `HEAD` method** requests the headers that would be returned if the `HEAD` request’s URL was instead requested with the HTTP `GET` method.

**Warning:** A response to a `HEAD` method *should not* have a body. If it has one anyway, that body **must be** ignored: any representation headers that might describe the erroneous body are instead assumed to describe the response which a similar `GET` request would have received.
